candidates.attacker_control: The `callback` (or fallback `c`) query-string parameter of a GET request to the SockJS `htmlfile`/`jsonp` endpoints is fully attacker-controlled. The value is read and used verbatim; no length, character, or format restriction is applied.
candidates.counterevidence_checked: Checked the routes, handler, listener, session-registration and template code for any validation, allow-list, quoting or escaping of the callback: none exists. escapeForJavaScript is applied only to message frame bodies, not to the callback. No CSP or X-Content-Type-Options headers are set by these responses, and the document is explicitly served as text/html with a UTF-8 charset, so no content sniffing is required. Confirmed the htmlfile/jsonp transports are enabled by default (SockJSHandlerOptions default disabledTransports empty) and that a frame is sent immediately on session creation. The JSONP-only variant was noted as lower impact because application/javascript does not execute as a document in the target origin.
candidates.impact: Reflected cross-site scripting in the origin of the Vert.x server. Because the response is a text/html document, script executed there runs with the application's origin and can act on behalf of a victim visiting the crafted URL (read non-HttpOnly cookies/DOM state, bypass CSRF protections, perform authenticated state-changing requests). The endpoint is cross-origin reachable and the payload is reflected on the first request, so no session prerequisite or user interaction beyond loading the URL/iframe is needed. The jsonp endpoint additionally allows arbitrary JavaScript to be injected into a JSONP response consumed by other origins.
candidates.prerequisites: The application registers SockJS via SockJSHandler.socketHandler(...)/bridge(...) on a router path. The HTML_FILE transport is enabled by default (SockJSHandlerOptions.disabledTransports is empty unless the operator disables it). No authentication or existing SockJS session is required: BaseTransport.getSession() creates the session for any path-supplied id, and SockJSSession.register() immediately calls writeOpen() -> sendFrame("o"), so the vulnerable frame is emitted on the first request. For the JsonP variant, impact is weaker because the response is application/javascript rather than a document type.
candidates.root_cause: SockJS fallback transports take the `callback`/`c` query parameter straight from `rc.request().getParam(...)` and splice it into generated markup/script without checking that it is a bare JavaScript identifier nor escaping it. HtmlFileTransport does `HTML_FILE_TEMPLATE.replace("{{ callback }}", callback)` inside `<script> ... var c = parent.{{ callback }}; ...` and sends it with Content-Type text/html (lines 90-97, 124-129); JsonPTransport does `callback + "(\"" + body + "\");"` with Content-Type application/javascript (lines 62-70, 149-159). BaseTransport only has `escapeForJavaScript` for message payloads (lines 94-102); no callback allow-list exists anywhere in the SockJS code.
candidates.title: Reflected XSS via unvalidated SockJS `callback` parameter in the htmlfile transport (same root cause in the jsonp transport)
candidates.trace: GET /<mount>/<server>/<session>/htmlfile?callback=<payload> -> SockJSHandlerImpl.handle -> sub-router regex COMMON_PATH_ELEMENT_RE + "htmlfile.*" -> HtmlFileTransport handler reads rc.request().getParam("callback") (HtmlFileTransport.java:90-97) -> new HtmlFileListener(..., callback, ...) -> session.register(...) (line 102) -> SockJSSession.register -> writeOpen -> listener.sendFrame("o") (SockJSSession.java:300-304, 403-405) -> HtmlFileListener.sendFrame -> HTML_FILE_TEMPLATE.replace("{{ callback }}", callback) with Content-Type text/html; charset=UTF-8 (HtmlFileTransport.java:121-131). The injected value sits directly inside a <script> element, so an attacker can terminate the script element and have arbitrary HTML/JS parsed and executed by the victim's browser in the target origin (e.g., when the URL is loaded in an iframe from an attacker page). JsonPTransport performs the equivalent concatenation at lines 157-163.
candidates.unverified: No runtime execution was performed: browser parsing/execution of an injected payload and the exact reflected response bytes were not observed, and I did not verify the corresponding upstream fix or CVE mapping. Severity depends on application usage (e.g., whether the SockJS routes are internet-reachable and whether session cookies are HttpOnly).
candidates.weakness_type: CWE-79 Improper Neutralization of Input During Web Page Generation (Reflected XSS); also CWE-116 output encoding

coverage_summary: Reviewed the assigned 244-file snapshot (vertx-web, vertx-web-common, vertx-web-client, vertx-web-api-contract, vertx-template-engines, vertx-sockjs-service-proxy) with read-only listing/search plus bounded file reads. In depth: all SockJS handler/transport/session classes, Utils/normalization/removeDots, StaticHandlerImpl, BodyHandlerImpl, Session/SessionHandler, Cookie/CookieHandler, CSRF/Basic/Digest/OAuth2/JWT auth handlers, RouterImpl/RouteImpl/RoutingContext/RoutingContextWrapper, HeaderParser, ErrorHandlerImpl, web-api-contract validation (BaseValidationHandler, XML/JSON validators, ParameterTypeValidator) and OpenAPI3 router factory/path resolver, web client core, and several template-engine loaders/implementations. Not exhaustively read: large javadoc package-info/example files, client-side JS (vertxbus.js/vertx-eventbus.js), Kotlin wrappers and generated converters, assembly/pom files and the sockjs-service-proxy annotations module (only skimmed).
limitations: No code was executed and no tests were run; there are no test sources in the provided snapshot, so all conclusions are static-reasoning leads, not runtime-confirmed vulnerabilities.
No dependency, build, container or deployment configuration analysis was performed; third-party frameworks (Netty, Jackson, Swagger parser, template engines) are outside the reviewed source.
Several security-relevant areas were only sampled (client-side JavaScript, Kotlin wrappers, generated converters, example/doc files), so additional issues there cannot be excluded.
The exact upstream CVE/fix mapping for this snapshot could not be verified offline, and the injected payload's browser behavior (e.g., CSP absence, iframe execution) was reasoned about, not observed.

rejected_leads.lead: StaticHandlerImpl path traversal (webRoot escape via encoded dots/slashes or Windows backslashes)
rejected_leads.reason: StaticHandlerImpl.handle() decodes and then re-runs Utils.removeDots() on the fully URL-decoded path, and removeDots never emits leading '..' segments, so POSIX traversal via %2e/%2f or double-encoding appears neutralized (Utils.removeDots, Utils.normalizePath). A Windows-only '\\' separator bypass (e.g., ..%5c) is plausible but platform-specific and was not runtime-verified; no cross-platform exploit path was established.

rejected_leads.lead: ErrorHandlerImpl renders exception/status messages into the HTML template without escaping (vertx-web-error.html, '{errorMessage}' replacement)
rejected_leads.reason: Requires the application to fail the context with an exception (or set a status message) containing attacker-influenced text while displayExceptionDetails is enabled (default true), so it is not directly reachable from framework-controlled input alone; the unescaped replacement also appears to be long-standing intended behavior rather than a distinct defect in this snapshot.

rejected_leads.lead: XMLTypeValidator uses a default DocumentBuilderFactory with no XXE hardening and calls parser.parse(String value) on the attacker-controlled request body (vertx-web-api-contract)
rejected_leads.reason: Reachable only when the application configures an XML body schema (addXMLBodySchema) and sends an XML content type. The parse(String) call is suspicious (system-id/URI semantics could give SSRF/file-read side effects) and external entity resolution is not disabled, but the practical exploitation path and Java parser semantics were not verified from source alone, so it was not selected as the single strongest candidate.

rejected_leads.lead: CSRFHandlerImpl token validation is not constant-time and the token is not bound to the session
rejected_leads.reason: Source shows signature comparison via String.equals and only MAC+timestamp verification, so a token obtained by an attacker elsewhere could be replayed for a different victim. This is a design weakness whose exploitability depends on how the application handles the token/header and on cross-site form submission, and no concrete bypass was demonstrated in this snapshot.

rejected_leads.lead: SockJS client-chosen session ids and missing WebSocket Origin checks allow cross-site session use
rejected_leads.reason: Session ids in the URL are chosen/guessed by the client and raw-WebSocket/SockJS endpoints do not validate Origin; these are inherent parts of the SockJS design and exploitation would require guessing an unguessable id, so no concrete hijack could be traced.

rejected_leads.lead: OAuth2AuthHandlerImpl reads but never validates the OAuth 'state' parameter
rejected_leads.reason: The handler passes the state through to the application; whether that is exploitable depends on application code that is not in this snapshot, so it is an integration weakness rather than a demonstrable framework vulnerability here.

rejected_leads.lead: SessionImpl cluster de-serialization of session data (ObjectInputStream/Class.newInstance) and session regeneration/lifecycle handling
rejected_leads.reason: Deserialization/cluster inputs are not attacker-controlled through the HTTP-facing code paths in this snapshot (session stores are populated by the application/cluster), and no external untrusted channel was established.

summary: One high-confidence source-level finding: the SockJS fallback transports embed the client-supplied `callback` request parameter into the response without any validation or output encoding. `HtmlFileTransport` writes it into a `text/html; charset=UTF-8` document that is placed in the response on the very first frame ("o") of a freshly created session, producing a cross-origin-reachable reflected XSS in the server's origin; `JsonPTransport` concatenates the same unvalidated value into an `application/javascript` response. Other areas reviewed (static handler path normalization, error handler, XML/JAXP body validation, CSRF/session/auth handlers, router/route matching, web client, API-contract) produced only weaker or unverified leads, listed as rejected.
